content: When introducing simulation training for the first time, it is highly beneficial to create a demonstration video tailored to the local context. This video should illustrate the proper use of the checklist, as it can significantly encourage team members to adopt it correctly. Observing teams during their use of the checklist and providing constructive feedback through coaching can further enhance their performance. To improve checklist visibility and usage, large posters displaying the checklist should be placed in areas accessible to all surgical team members. Additionally, fostering a culture of safety and teamwork within the organization is crucial. This can be achieved by forming a multidisciplinary team to lead the project at each site, which promotes communication and a sense of ownership among staff. Regular discussions about the checklist and its implementation during staff and physician meetings can help integrate it into the local culture. Modifying the checklist to align with local practices, such as adding items like deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis, can make it more relevant and effective. The World Health Organization (WHO) has supported checklist implementation by creating an online community to gather feedback and engage users. This virtual platform allowed implementers to share experiences and report barriers, such as clinician resistance (especially from surgeons), lack of resources, insufficient education on checklist use, and resource constraints. Modifying the checklist to include local hospital names and logos has been shown to increase buy-in and adoption. Key influencers, such as national governments and WHO country offices, have played a significant role in promoting the checklist. Many governments have mandated its use in public healthcare facilities, often through health ministries. Mandates with consequences, such as financial incentives or regulatory certifications, have been more effective than unenforced mandates. Voluntary implementation efforts have also been successful, often driven by professional societies, hospital associations, and non-governmental organizations. These efforts rely on systematic awareness campaigns, local champions, and resource support to encourage adoption. Voluntary programs benefit from engaging clinicians, fostering ownership, and addressing local needs. Educational initiatives should be delivered in multiple formats, such as webinars, in-person meetings, and skills training sessions, to reach a broad audience. Interactive webinars can engage participants by polling their experiences and encouraging dialogue. In-person meetings provide opportunities for peer learning and re-energizing participants. Skills training, such as teamwork and communication exercises specific to the operating room, can further enhance the checklist's effectiveness. Coaching visits to facilities can provide direct support to local teams, offering feedback and building relationships. These visits should be conducted multiple times during the program to monitor progress and address challenges. Data collection for monitoring should be streamlined to avoid overburdening facilities, and existing processes should be leveraged where possible. At the facility level, implementing the checklist requires a cultural shift, as it often involves changes to workflows and communication practices. Facilities should start small, test the checklist in simulation settings, and gradually expand its use. Leadership teams should review and customize the checklist to fit local needs, ensuring it is relevant and practical. Continuous support, education, and monitoring are essential to maintain its use and effectiveness over time.
